claim_revisions.subject: Quantitative results in the 2016 Nature article on a quantum speed limit with computer games, by Sørensen and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 22 July 2020, Nature published a retraction note by Sørensen and co-authors on their 2016 article. The authors state that an error in their computer code means the quantitative results reported are not valid.

evidence.quote: Retraction Note: Exploring the quantum speed limit with computer games
We, the authors, are regretfully retracting this Article owing to an error in our computer code that means the quantitative results reported are not valid.

claim_revisions.subject: The 2017 Nature article on epitaxy of nanowire quantum devices by Gazibegovic and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 19 April 2022, Gazibegovic and co-authors published a retraction note in Nature on their 2017 article. The note states that unjustified data removal and cropping affect the agreement between the theoretical curves and the experimental data and the claims of ballistic transport, and that the authors are retracting the paper.

evidence.quote: We found unjustified data removal and cropping in Figures 4a and c, and Extended Data Figures 7 and 8, which affect the agreement between the theoretical curves and the experimental data and the claims of ballistic transport.
We are accordingly retracting the paper.

claim_revisions.subject: Labels in Fig. 3a of the 9 December 2024 Nature article by Google Quantum AI and Collaborators
claim_revisions.statement: On 28 April 2026, Nature published an author correction to the 9 December 2024 article by Google Quantum AI and Collaborators. The correction states that the Fig. 3a x-axis label now reads “Repetition code distance, d” and originally appeared as “Surface code distance, d,”.

evidence.quote: there were errors in Fig. 3a, where the x-axis label, now reading “Repetition code distance, d”originally appeared as “Surface code distance, d,” while in the Fig. 3a keys, the open and closed circles, now reading “Ref. 17” and “This work,” respectively, were originally denoted “d = 3 (ref. 17)” and “d = 5.”

claim_revisions.subject: X-axis units on a graph in the 6 May 2024 Nature article by Réglade and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 17 May 2024, Nature published an author correction to the 6 May 2024 article by Réglade and co-authors. The correction states that in the uppermost graph of Fig. 3d the x-axis units were erroneously listed as μs instead of ms.

evidence.quote: in the uppermost graph of Fig. 3d, the x-axis units were erroneously listed as μs instead of ms.

claim_revisions.subject: Sampling the output distribution of the Sycamore circuits in the 23 October 2019 Nature article by Arute and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 28 August 2022, Pan, Chen and Zhang posted a preprint on sampling the output distribution of the Sycamore circuits in the 23 October 2019 Nature article by Arute and co-authors. Pan, Chen and Zhang state that those circuits have “been used to demonstrate quantum supremacy.” Arute and co-authors state that the Sycamore result “is an experimental realization of quantum supremacy”. The preprint’s arXiv record lists the journal reference Physical Review Letters 129, 090502 (2022).

evidence.quote: which is believed to be beyond the reach of classical supercomputers and has been used to demonstrate quantum supremacy.
is an experimental realization of quantum supremacy

Our Sycamore processor takes about 200 seconds to sample one instance of a quantum circuit a million times—our benchmarks currently indicate that the equivalent task for a state-of-the-art classical supercomputer would take approximately 10,000 years.

claim_revisions.subject: Classical simulation of the kicked Ising experiment in the 14 June 2023 Nature article by Kim and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 26 January 2024, Tindall, Fishman, Stoudenmire and Sels posted a preprint reporting a classical simulation of the kicked Ising experiment in the 14 June 2023 Nature article by Kim and co-authors. Kim and co-authors state that the experiments represent “evidence for the utility of quantum computing in a pre-fault-tolerant era.” Tindall, Fishman, Stoudenmire and Sels state that their classical simulation “is significantly more accurate and precise than the results obtained from the quantum processor.” The preprint’s arXiv record lists the journal reference PRX Quantum 5, 010308 (2024).

evidence.quote: A simulation of this system was recently performed on a 127 qubit quantum processor
we can perform a classical simulation that is significantly more accurate and precise than the results obtained from the quantum processor and many other classical methods.
We argue that this represents evidence for the utility of quantum computing in a pre-fault-tolerant era.
Here we report experiments on a noisy 127-qubit processor and demonstrate the measurement of accurate expectation values for circuit volumes at a scale beyond brute-force classical computation.

claim_revisions.subject: Classical simulation by Begušić, Gray and Chan of the kicked Ising experiment in the 14 June 2023 Nature article by Kim and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 26 January 2024, Begušić, Gray and Chan posted a preprint on a classical simulation of the kicked Ising experiment in the 14 June 2023 Nature article by Kim and co-authors. Kim and co-authors state that the experiments represent “evidence for the utility of quantum computing in a pre-fault-tolerant era.” Begušić, Gray and Chan state that approximate classical methods “can simulate these observables orders of magnitude faster than the quantum experiment.” The preprint’s arXiv record lists the journal reference Sci. Adv. 10, eadk4321 (2024).

evidence.quote: can simulate these observables orders of magnitude faster than the quantum experiment
We argue that this represents evidence for the utility of quantum computing in a pre-fault-tolerant era.
Here we report experiments on a noisy 127-qubit processor and demonstrate the measurement of accurate expectation values for circuit volumes at a scale beyond brute-force classical computation.

claim_revisions.subject: Classical simulation of Gaussian boson sampling experiments, including Borealis and the photon experiment by Zhong and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 25 June 2024, Nature Physics published a paper whose landing page is titled “Classical algorithm for simulating experimental Gaussian boson sampling.” Oh and co-authors state that they “simulate the largest Borealis, Jiuzhang2.0, and Jiuzhang3.0 experiments, which were used to claim quantum computational advantage” and that the simulation “disputes the experimental quantum advantage claims.” Madsen and co-authors state “Here we report quantum computational advantage using Borealis”. Zhong and co-authors report the title “Quantum computational advantage using photons”.

evidence.quote: Classical algorithm for simulating experimental Gaussian boson sampling
which disputes the experimental quantum advantage claims.
We now simulate the largest Borealis, Jiuzhang2.0, and Jiuzhang3.0 experiments, which were used to claim quantum computational advantage.
Here we report quantum computational advantage using Borealis, a photonic processor offering dynamic programmability on all gates implemented.

claim_revisions.subject: A neural-network comparison in the article by King and co-authors
claim_revisions.statement: On 9 July 2026, Krinitsin, Alert, Rizzi and Schmitt posted a preprint comment on the article by King and co-authors. King and co-authors state that “neural networks cannot achieve the same accuracy as the quantum annealer within a reasonable time frame.” The comment states that “NQS can provide competitive results in some of the cases”. The article’s arXiv record lists the journal reference Science 388, 199-204 (2025).

evidence.quote: NQS can provide competitive results in some of the cases when accounting for the Monte-Carlo noise and large autocorrelation times between samples obtained from the final state.
neural networks cannot achieve the same accuracy as the quantum annealer within a reasonable time frame.

gaps.topic: Quantized Majorana conductance retraction and expression of concern
gaps.why: The 8 March 2021 Nature retraction (10.1038/s41586-021-03373-x) and the 29 April 2020 editorial expression of concern (10.1038/s41586-020-2252-6) of the 2018 article Quantized Majorana conductance (10.1038/nature26142) are assigned to history_other.json. They are not recorded here.
gaps.would_need: Nothing further in this file. history_other should carry both notices for that article.

gaps.topic: Expression of concern on the quantum speed limit article
gaps.why: Nature published an editorial expression of concern, DOI 10.1038/s41586-020-2274-0, dated 2020-05-05 in the article HTML schema.org block, on the same 2016 article later retracted. The HTML description was empty, the PDF URL returned HTML rather than a PDF, and the PubMed record had no abstract, so the notice body was not in the fetched text.
gaps.would_need: The notice PDF or another publisher copy that contains the expression-of-concern paragraph.

gaps.topic: Journal PDFs refused for three classical-simulation papers
gaps.why: journals.aps.org returned 403 for the Pan and Tindall PDFs and abstract pages. science.org returned 403 for the Begušić PDF. The quoted sentences are from the arXiv PDFs. Each arXiv abstract page lists a journal reference: Physical Review Letters 129, 090502 (2022); PRX Quantum 5, 010308 (2024); Sci. Adv. 10, eadk4321 (2024). Those journal pages were not used for the scientific quotes.
gaps.would_need: The journal PDF or HTML body, fetched under the declared User-Agent, so the quotes can be checked against the journal text.

gaps.topic: Nature Physics body for the Gaussian boson sampling paper
gaps.why: The Nature Physics landing page for 10.1038/s41567-024-02535-8 returned the title and datePublished 2024-06-25. The PDF URL returned the same HTML shell, not the article body. The scientific sentences are from arXiv:2306.03709v2, dated 4 Dec 2023 on the PDF.
gaps.would_need: The Nature Physics PDF, to confirm the journal text matches the preprint sentences.

gaps.why: Oh and co-authors name Borealis, Jiuzhang2.0 and Jiuzhang3.0. This file quotes the Borealis article and the Zhong preprint whose arXiv record lists Science 370, 1460 (2020). The later two experiments are quoted only in Oh and co-authors' sentence.
gaps.would_need: The articles that report Jiuzhang2.0 and Jiuzhang3.0, so their own wording can be quoted.

gaps.topic: IBM secondary-storage preprint on Sycamore circuits
gaps.why: arXiv:1910.09534, by Pednault and co-authors at IBM, estimates a classical simulation of 53- and 54-qubit Sycamore circuits and states that the computations were not carried out. It was not recorded as a published rebuttal. The accompanying IBM Research blog was not used.
gaps.would_need: A journal version, or a later paper by the same authors reporting that the estimated simulation was run.

gaps.topic: Publisher corrections that do not revise a reported result
gaps.why: Two publisher corrections were fetched and not recorded. 10.1038/s41586-026-10108-3 (19 January 2026), on the article by Bluvstein and co-authors, changes one Fig. 3d label from “corrected decoding” to “correlated decoding”. 10.1038/s41524-025-01513-9 (21 January 2026) adds omitted affiliations on the Quantinuum and BMW catalyst article.
gaps.would_need: Nothing, unless a later notice revises a reported result in either article.

gaps.topic: Science PDF of the King and co-authors article
gaps.why: The Krinitsin comment and the arXiv record identify the article as Science 388, 199-204 (2025). The quoted King sentence is from arXiv:2403.00910v2, whose abstract page says it was last revised 14 Oct 2025. The Science PDF was not fetched.
gaps.would_need: The Science PDF, to confirm that sentence is in the journal text.
